Lesson six! A container is like a small Linux machine. Today you'll open a shell inside the running engine x, look around, change its welcome page, and see your change in the browser.
First, start engine x.
Start engine x in the background, named web, reachable at localhost port eighty eighty. Pause the video, type it yourself, then continue.
docker run, dash d, dash dash name web, dash p, eighty eighty colon eighty, engine x. Engine x is running.
Open localhost port eighty eighty and keep the tab open. You should see, Welcome to engine x.
Now, let's go inside.
Type docker exec, dash i t, web, bash. And look, the prompt changed.
Exec means execute. It runs a command inside a container that is already running.
Dash i t means interactive plus terminal, so you can type into it. You need it for a shell.
And bash is the command to run. It's a shell.
Your prompt changed. You are now inside the container, as root. The name after the at sign is the container's I D.
Let's look around. Engine x serves its web pages from the folder slash user slash share slash engine x slash H T M L.
List it with L S. There are two files: fifty x dot H T M L, and index dot H T M L.
Now print the home page with cat. It's H T M L, with the title, Welcome to engine x.
That's exactly the page you see in the browser.
Now let's change the page.
Type echo, then the text, Hello from my container, inside an h one tag, then a greater than sign, and the path to index dot H T M L.
Echo prints the text, and the greater than sign writes it into the file instead of the screen, replacing what was there.
Now reload the browser tab. Hello from my container! That's your page!
Note the single quotes around the text. With double quotes, the exclamation mark confuses the shell, and you get, event not found. Single quotes pass the text exactly as written.
Here's a question. Why not just open the file in nano?
Let's try. nano, and the file path. Oh. bash says, nano, command not found.
The engine x image has no nano, and no v i. Images are kept small, so they only contain what the app needs.
Now let's come back out.
Type exit. And your normal prompt is back.
Is the container still running? List the running containers. Pause the video, type it yourself, then continue.
docker P S. Yes, web is still up.
Exit closed only the shell that exec started, not the container. The browser still shows your page. It's like Control C on docker logs dash f, in lesson five.
Now, a question. If you stop and start the container again, is your change still there?
Stop the container. Pause the video, type it yourself, then continue.
docker stop web. The container is stopped, but its index file still has your Hello page.
Reload the browser. Engine x isn't running, so there's no page. But the container still exists, only stopped. Remember docker P S dash a, from lesson three.
So let's start the same container again, with docker start web.
Reload, and there it is! Your change is still there. Stopping a container doesn't delete it, so its files are kept.
Docker start restarts an existing container, with the same name, port, and files. Docker run always creates a new one.
But what happens if you delete the container, and run it again? Where does your change go?
Stop and delete web in one command. Pause the video, type it yourself, then continue.
docker R M, dash f, web. The container is deleted.
Now create a new one, exactly like in step one. Pause the video, type it yourself, then continue.
docker run, dash d, dash dash name web, dash p, eighty eighty colon eighty, engine x. A new container is running.
Reload the browser. Welcome to engine x. Oh no, your page is gone!
Why is it gone? Because you changed the container, not the image. The engine x image always says, Welcome to engine x.
Your change, Hello from my container, lived in the old container.
Then docker R M deleted that container, and your change with it.
Docker run made a new container, a fresh copy of the image. Every new container starts from the image, which never changed.
So, docker stop, then docker start, keeps your change, because it's the same container. But docker R M, then docker run, loses it, because it's a new container from the image.
So, changes made inside a container live only as long as the container. Lesson eight shows how to keep your changes. For now, let's clean up.
Stop and delete web in one command. Pause the video, type it yourself, then continue.
docker R M, dash f, web. All clean.

Awesome! You went inside a container! docker exec, dash i t, name, bash, opens a shell inside a running container. Exit leaves the shell, and the container keeps running. docker start starts a stopped container again, with your changes. But changes are lost when the container is deleted.
